transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Liam Ortiz (AE), Maria Chen (SE), Omar Patel (Solutions Eng)
Attendees (Customer): Nina Rao (Head of ML), Jared Kim (Platform Engineer), Priya Singh (SRE), Elliot Park (PM)
Recording note: auto transcription, medium quality, some proper nouns garbled

Summary:
Quick scoping for POC benchmark harness integration. Main goals: validate streaming vs non-streaming throughput and latency for AstraEdge's NER + summarization workloads, agree success criteria (p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, end-to-end tail latency with prefix caching), and align on deliverables for sample adapter and test scripts. Discussed concurrency envelope, payload size distribution, and a short timeline for pilot runs.

Topics covered:
- Harness adapter work: python/node examples, auth and routing
- Streaming vs non-streaming test cases (server-side stream, client read patterns)
- Workload sizing: token distributions, prompt prefixes, KV cache warmup
- Metrics & success criteria: p50/p90/p99 latency, cold vs warm start, token cost, error rate
- Rollout/timeline and gating criteria for production-ready Dedicated option

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour. quick intros — i'm liam from redwood, maria and omar are with me — we'll run through the harness plan, and make sure we have the scripts you need.
[00:12] Nina Rao: thanks liam. nina here. Our goal is to get a pilot that proves we can hit 150ms p99 for short summarization requests and keep cost under our current internal baseline. we'll share the scripts after.
[00:25] Jared Kim: hey all, jared — platform. high level for us is traffic profile: steady 30 qps during business hours, 250 qps peak for 10 min bursts, typical payloads: 1) short prompts ~150 tokens, 2) medium ~600 tokens, 3) long ~2k tokens.
[00:42] Maria Chen: got it. that helps. when you say summarization, is that single-turn or multi-turn with long context?
[00:48] Nina Rao: mostly single-turn summarization of meeting notes, but we also have an NER pipeline that uses streaming tokens to extract entities as they stream in — so we want to test both streaming APIs and non-streaming generation.
[01:01] Omar Patel: just to clarify, streaming in the harness will simulate chunked client reads and measure first-byte latency and time-to-complete, right?
[01:08] Priya Singh: yes, sres care about tail for first byte, because our UI shows partial results. if streaming is too bursty it affects user experience.
[01:16] Liam Ortiz: okay, so two parallel benchmark axes: throughput/latency for non-stream full responses, and incremental latency & throughput for streaming. We'll prototype a harness adapter that can run both patterns against Redwood hosted and then a Dedicated sim.

[01:32] Jared Kim: couple questions. 1) how do you want the customer scripts? should they be a straight curl wrapper, or do you want our internal client library? 2) how do you handle KV cache warmup for the streaming case?
[01:45] Maria Chen: great q. For the harness we prefer straight python/node examples that call the raw API so there's no magic client-side caching interfering. For KV cache warmup we can run an initial ramp (a set of prefix-only calls) and mark that phase as warmup, then run steady-state. We'll log cache-hit ratios where possible.
[02:02] Elliot Park: is it possible to test with prefixes that are shared across many requests? that's more realistic for us.
[02:08] Maria Chen: yes, we typically include a "shared prefix" bucket in the workloads so the harness can measure prefix cache hit impact on cost and latency.
[02:15] Nina Rao: ok good. success criteria — beyond p99 — we also want an SLA-like metric: error rate under 0.2% and cold start tail under 500ms for the flow that uses dedicated pools.
[02:28] Liam Ortiz: noted. we'll codify success criteria in the bench run plan doc. we'll also include per-route token costs so you can compare to your internal baseline.

[03:00] [timestamp drift/brief crosstalk] Jared Kim: and what about batching? we rely on small batch sizes, but during peaks we do micro-batching at the client side. do you simulate different batch distributions?
[03:12] Maria Chen: yes, harness supports configurable batch size distributions. We can run three scenarios: single-infer (no batching), small batch (2-8), and larger batch (8-32). We'll capture latency percentiles for each.
[03:25] Priya Singh: can the harness model client backpressure? our frontend uses windowed reads and sometimes stalls.
[03:31] Omar Patel: we have a mode that simulates read throttling and random slow consumers; it will surface how the server-side handles stalled drains and if there are memory retention issues.
[03:40] Elliot Park: also, we need to ensure the harness preserves header-level metadata for tracing and includes sampling for traces.
[03:46] Maria Chen: yep we include an option to inject trace headers and sample at 1% by default. we can bump it higher for the pilot.

[04:10] Nina Rao: timeline question: how long for you to produce the sample adapter and walkthrough?
[04:15] Maria Chen: i can have python + node adapters in ~4 business days, with a README and a small docker-compose that runs a local harness runner. so target 2025-11-10.
[04:25] Liam Ortiz: perfect — we'll also include a short bench plan: warmup -> steady -> burst -> cooldown, and produce a results template for you to fill.
[04:35] Jared Kim: on the dataset side, we'll provide a synthetic set with token histograms. do you accept compressed samples?
[04:42] Maria Chen: gzip is fine; prefer a small sample first (50-200 items) for quick sanity runs, then a larger set for full runs.

[05:10] [Long section of technical clarifications, timestamps approximated every ~30s] 
[05:10] Maria Chen: for streaming we capture two additional metrics: time-to-first-chunk (TTFC) and incremental token latency (avg per-chunk). We'll also measure memory and open connection counts on the host.
[05:22] Priya Singh: memory behavior is critical for us — can the harness drive sustained streams with 2k token contexts and observe memory growth?
[05:30] Omar Patel: yes, we'll instrument the runtime with a small agent to emit memory RSS at 5s intervals — that will detect leaks and retention when many streams are open.
[05:40] Jared Kim: how about certificates/auth? our staging uses mTLS for internal endpoints. can the adapter support it?
[05:47] Maria Chen: sample adapter will include TLS + token auth patterns. mTLS we can support; might need a bit of extra config from your side (certs and a test CA).
[05:56] Nina Rao: can you also show how quantized models change perf? some of our models will be int8 quantized for Dedicated nodes.
[06:03] Maria Chen: absolutely. we can run the same harness against a quantized variant and report delta on latency & token cost. We will also recommend kernel configs depending on observed sequence lengths.
[06:15] Elliot Park: are there hard limits on concurrency per model instance? we need to know when to scale out vs scale up.
[06:21] Omar Patel: we provide guidance based on observed throughput per GPU/instance; part of the bench report will recommend concurrency caps and instance sizing to meet your p99 targets.
[06:30] Nina Rao: what about error modes — e.g., truncated tokens, partial outputs, occasional 500s — do you inject faults?
[06:38] Maria Chen: we can run a fault-injection pass that simulates 0.1-1% transient errors and measure retry behavior and end-to-end user impact. good for resilience tests.
[06:48] Jared Kim: please also include a CSV with raw timings so our SRE can run custom analysis.
[06:52] Maria Chen: yes — raw CSV, aggregated summary, and an artifacts bundle with flamegraphs for CPU-bound runs.
[07:00] Liam Ortiz: ok next, success criteria recap — nina suggested: p99 <=150ms for short summarization, error rate <0.2%, cold start <500ms for dedicated, memory stable under sustained streaming. Anything else?
[07:12] Priya Singh: include cost metric: total token cost per 1M tokens and relative to current infra (we'll provide baseline cost).
[07:18] Nina Rao: add observability — trace sampling, token-level cost breakdown by route.
[07:24] Liam Ortiz: added. we'll draft the bench plan with those gates.

[07:45] [Wrap-up and next steps]
[07:45] Liam Ortiz: to summarize action items — maria will produce the adapters and transcribe steps in the repo; nina and jared will give scripts, payload distributions and certs if mTLS is needed; liam will send pilot contract & pricing. we'll schedule the follow-up bench sync for next week.
[07:59] Nina Rao: thanks liam, appreciate the clarity. one ask — can you include a sample config that mimics our peak 10-min burst pattern?
[08:06] Maria Chen: yes we'll include a burst pattern config (ramp to 250 qps over 30s, sustain 10 min, then decay).
[08:12] Liam Ortiz: great. we'll aim to have first smoke runs inside 10 days once we get scripts. thanks everyone.
[08:20] Jared Kim: thanks, bye.

Post-call notes:
- artifacts referenced: sample adapter repo link (to be shared), bench plan template (drive link placeholder), measurement CSV template.
- possible gotcha flagged by customer: mTLS and SSO traces for dedicated deployment, ensure cert handoff early.
- suggested pilot: 2-week bench window with one day warmup, three full-run permutations (streaming, non-streaming small batch, non-streaming large batch).

End of transcript.
